Failures in Agentic AI

A five-dimension taxonomy and an empirical analysis of 3,089 publicly reported failures across eight agent orchestration frameworks. Every record below can be traced to its original report.

What this study found

Four results, each with the evidence that supports it.

Most failures are interface failures. The three categories that describe a break between components — compatibility and API contracts, output parsing, and tool integration — account for 43.9% of records. The two categories unique to multi-agent architectures, communication and context, account for 8.4%. Orchestration failures are real and measurable, but they are not the plurality.

Cause is associated with type, but the causal evidence is thin. Type and stated cause are strongly associated (Cramér's V = 0.373, χ² = 3878, p < 1e-12), yet only 374 records (12.1%) name a checkable mechanism. The rest are graded supported or hypothesised, and no causal claim in this study rests on them.

Frameworks fail differently, not worse. Composition differs (V = 0.261) and no two frameworks share a dominant category. Blocking-severity rate ranges from 36.5% to 96.0% — a property of how loudly a framework fails, not of its quality.

About a third of failures are silent. 31.9% were not detected by the framework runtime and reached the user as incorrect output rather than as an error. This is the strongest argument in the study for output validation over exception monitoring.

The codebook

Five dimensions, coded independently. Every category below has a definition, an inclusion list and an exclusion list, so that two coders can reach the same label from the same text. Click a category to expand it.

The dimensions are orthogonal on purpose: a compatibility failure can be caused by a framework defect, a version bump or a user misconfiguration, and those have different remediations. Collapsing them is why "agent errors" reports rarely generalise.

A. Failure type

What broke, structurally — 10 categories

Structural signals (tool invocation, inter-agent handoff, output parsing, environment setup) outrank generic complaint language. When a report contains a traceback, the raising component decides the label. Generic phrases such as "does not work" never override a structural signal.
A1_functionality — Functionality / reasoning defect
The agent architecture ran as designed but produced an incorrect result: wrong answer, wrong plan, wrong code, wrong decision, or an incomplete task outcome.
Includes:
  • Output is wrong but syntactically well formed
  • Plan or delegation choice is logically incorrect
  • Agent silently skips part of the requested task
Excludes:
  • A specific component raised an exception (code that category)
  • The reported problem is purely about installation or configuration
A2_tool_integration — Tool / integration defect
Failure in the interface between the agent and an external capability: tool registration, tool selection, argument construction, MCP server connection, or tool result handling.
Includes:
  • Tool not found / not registered / not exposed to the model
  • Arguments built wrongly for a tool call
  • MCP server, plugin or connector fails to load
  • Tool returns a value the agent cannot consume
Excludes:
  • The tool works but the agent chose the wrong tool (code A1)
A3_compatibility — Compatibility / API-contract defect
A mismatch between component versions, or between the framework's expected interface and the installed/upstream interface. Includes breaking changes, removed parameters, renamed symbols and dependency conflicts.
Includes:
  • TypeError on an unexpected or missing keyword argument
  • ImportError / ModuleNotFoundError for a moved or renamed symbol
  • Version pin conflict between framework and dependency
  • Deprecated parameter removed upstream
Excludes:
  • A user-supplied value of the wrong type with correct API (code A6)
A4_communication — Agent communication / orchestration defect
Failure originating in the exchange between agents: message routing, handoff, delegation, speaker selection, turn taking, termination, or shared-conversation state.
Includes:
  • Handoff or delegation never occurs, or targets the wrong agent
  • Conversation loops, never terminates, or terminates early
  • Manager/supervisor misroutes a task
  • Agents disagree and no resolution mechanism applies
Excludes:
  • A single agent fails alone with no inter-agent exchange (code A1/A2)
A5_context_memory — Context / memory / state defect
Failure caused by what the agent could see or remember: context truncation, lost history, memory persistence errors, or corrupted run state.
Includes:
  • Earlier instructions dropped from the context window
  • Memory store returns stale or cross-session data
  • Checkpoint/resume restores an inconsistent state
Excludes:
  • The context was present but the model ignored it (code A1)
A6_data_structure — Data structure / output-parsing defect
The agent produced output whose structure was unusable: schema validation failure, JSON parsing failure, type mismatch, or serialisation error. Includes the supervisor's "data structure failures".
Includes:
  • Pydantic/JSON schema validation error on agent output
  • Output parser cannot extract the expected block
  • KeyError / AttributeError on a malformed payload
Excludes:
  • Parsing failed because the tool was never called (code A2)
A7_configuration — Configuration / environment defect
Failure in setup rather than in agent behaviour: missing environment variables, credentials, settings, install steps, container setup, or unsupported runtime.
Includes:
  • Missing API key or environment variable
  • Installation or dependency resolution fails before any agent runs
  • Configuration option ignored or has no effect
Excludes:
  • Version incompatibility between packages (code A3)
A8_performance — Performance / resource defect
Failure of completion due to resource or timing limits: timeouts, rate limits, memory exhaustion, excessive token consumption, or prohibitive latency.
Includes:
  • Request times out or is killed by a deadline
  • Provider rate limit reached
  • Run exhausts memory or token budget
Excludes:
  • Slow but correct completion with no failure (not a record)
A9_safety — Safety / guardrail defect
Failure of control rather than capability: unsafe action executed, permission boundary crossed, prompt injection accepted, or guardrail bypassed.
Includes:
  • Agent executes a destructive action it should not
  • Injected instruction from tool output is followed
  • Sandbox or permission restriction is not enforced
Excludes:
  • Policy refusal that is merely inconvenient (code A1)
A10_unknown — Insufficient evidence
The report does not contain enough information to assign a category. Retained in the dataset and reported explicitly; never silently dropped.
Includes:
  • Title-only report with no described symptom
  • Report describes a question or feature request rather than a failure
Excludes:
  • The report names a mechanism that supports any other category
  • The text is a feature request, question or documentation note rather than a failure, which is excluded from the corpus instead of coded here

B. Cause class

The mechanism the report names — 10 categories

B1_framework_defect — Framework defect
A bug in the orchestration framework's own code.
Includes:
  • The fault is in the framework's own code path
  • A maintainer confirms the defect or links a fix
  • The same input fails only on one framework version
Excludes:
  • The user's own agent code is at fault (B8)
  • An upstream provider changed its API (B2)
B2_api_version_drift — API / version drift
A change in an upstream dependency or framework version broke an existing application.
Includes:
  • Behaviour changes after an upgrade of the framework or a provider SDK
  • A renamed, removed or newly required argument breaks existing code
  • Pinning an older version resolves the report
Excludes:
  • The version was never compatible with the documented requirement (B3)
  • A bug present in all versions of the framework (B1)
B3_configuration_error — Configuration error
Incorrect or missing configuration by the application developer.
Includes:
  • A required key, variable, path or credential is absent or malformed
  • Installation, dependency resolution or container setup is incomplete
  • The same code succeeds once the environment is corrected
Excludes:
  • A missing internal symbol raised by an otherwise working install (B1)
  • An external service that is down rather than misconfigured (B7)
B4_specification_ambiguity — Specification / documentation ambiguity
The documented behaviour is unclear, absent, or contradicted the actual behaviour.
Includes:
  • The documented behaviour does not state what the reporter assumed
  • Two reasonable readings of the API lead to the reported failure
  • The fix is a documentation change rather than a code change
Excludes:
  • The documentation is clear and the user misread it (B9)
  • Nothing is documented because the feature does not exist (B9)
B5_model_limitation — Model capability limitation
The underlying model could not perform the required reasoning or instruction following.
Includes:
  • The task is beyond the model's capability at the stated size or budget
  • Output quality degrades with a known model weakness such as arithmetic
  • The same prompt succeeds with a stronger model
Excludes:
  • The model was given the wrong instructions (B8)
  • The model was denied relevant context it could have used (B6)
B6_context_management — Context / state mismanagement
Information needed for the task was not preserved, routed, or restored.
Includes:
  • History, retrieved context or shared state is dropped or truncated
  • The agent forgets an earlier instruction within the same run
  • A checkpoint or resume path loses state
Excludes:
  • The prompt as assembled was already wrong before any loss (B8)
  • The provider rejected an oversized request (B7)
B7_tool_environment — Tool or environment unavailability
An external dependency was unavailable, misbehaving, or unconfigured.
Includes:
  • A tool, service or network dependency is unavailable or rate limited
  • The sandbox, filesystem or interpreter cannot perform the call
  • The failure disappears when the dependency is restored
Excludes:
  • The tool works but was called with wrong arguments (B8)
  • The tool is not installed because setup was incomplete (B3)
B8_application_logic — Application logic defect
The defect is in the developer's own agent code, not the framework or model.
Includes:
  • The user's own orchestration, prompt or glue code is incorrect
  • A wrong default, branch or loop bound is visible in the report
  • Correcting the application code resolves the failure
Excludes:
  • The framework itself behaves contrary to its documentation (B1)
  • The application is correct but the model cannot do the task (B5)
B9_expectation_mismatch — Expectation mismatch
The behaviour is by design; the reporter expected something else.
Includes:
  • The reported behaviour is the documented or intended behaviour
  • The feature is unsupported and the report is a request for it
  • Maintainers close the report as expected behaviour
Excludes:
  • The documentation genuinely contradicts the behaviour (B4)
  • The failure is real and the cause is a defect (B1 or B8)
B10_unknown — Unknown
No cause recoverable from the report.
Includes:
  • No mechanism is stated and none can be inferred from the text
  • The cause is recorded as hypothesised rather than identified
Excludes:
  • Any category above is supported by the text, however briefly

C. Lifecycle stage

Where in the run it broke — 8 categories

C1_setup — Installation, dependency resolution, environment or credentials
The failure occurred before any agent code ran: installing the package, resolving dependencies, or satisfying an environment or credential precondition.
Includes:
  • Dependency resolution or package installation fails
  • A credential, API key or environment variable is absent at start-up
  • A required system library or container layer is missing
Excludes:
  • A framework-internal symbol is missing in an otherwise working install (compatibility, dimension A)
  • A model call fails after start-up succeeded (C4)
C2_construction — Building agents, teams, graphs, or tools before execution
Building the objects that define the workflow - agents, teams, graphs, tools, routers - failed, or the object was constructed in an invalid configuration.
Includes:
  • An agent, team or graph constructor raises
  • Tool registration or its schema is rejected at build time
  • An invalid graph topology is rejected before execution
Excludes:
  • Credentials or dependencies are missing before construction (C1)
  • An agent-to-agent exchange fails after the workflow is running (C6)
C3_prompt_assembly — Assembling task description, roles, or context for a call
The failure occurred while composing the input to a model call: system prompt, role descriptions, the message list, or retrieved context.
Includes:
  • A prompt template renders incorrectly or with missing fields
  • Assembled context exceeds the window before the request is sent
  • The message list is malformed before it reaches the provider
Excludes:
  • Context is lost between calls during the run (dimension A: context and memory)
  • The provider rejects the request after it was sent (C4)
C4_inference — The model call itself
The failure occurred in the model call itself: the provider rejected the request, the response was unusable, or the response content is wrong.
Includes:
  • The provider returns an error, times out, or rate limits the call
  • The model returns an incomplete, wrong or hallucinated answer
  • The token limit is hit during generation
Excludes:
  • Composing the request failed before sending (C3)
  • A well-formed response could not be parsed into the expected schema (C7)
C5_tool_execution — Invoking or receiving from a tool or external service
The failure occurred at the tool boundary: the wrong tool was selected, its arguments were wrong, it was unavailable, or its result was unusable.
Includes:
  • The selected tool does not exist or is not registered at call time
  • Arguments fail the tool's own schema
  • The external service returns an error to the tool
Excludes:
  • A tool object could not be constructed at all (C2)
  • The tool returned successfully and parsing its result failed (C7)
C6_handoff — Passing control or state between agents
Passing control or state between agents failed: the wrong agent was selected, the handoff never happened, or the message was rejected by the receiver.
Includes:
  • Speaker selection loops or picks the same agent repeatedly
  • A delegation never returns to the caller
  • The receiving agent rejects the handoff payload
Excludes:
  • A single agent looping with no second agent (C4)
  • State is lost between calls inside one agent (C3)
C7_output_parsing — Interpreting or validating the model's structured output
A response was produced but could not be interpreted or validated: malformed JSON, a schema violation, a missing key, or a wrong type.
Includes:
  • JSON decoding of model output fails
  • Pydantic or JSON-schema validation fails on the response
  • A required key is absent or mistyped in structured output
Excludes:
  • Arguments fail validation while being sent to a tool (C5)
  • The response parses correctly but states the wrong answer (C4)
C8_runtime_other — Other runtime behaviour after a successful call
The failure occurred in runtime behaviour not covered above, after at least one successful call: orchestration bookkeeping, scheduling, logging, or teardown.
Includes:
  • Framework bookkeeping raises after a successful call
  • Cleanup or teardown fails at the end of a run
  • The behaviour fits no earlier stage on this list
Excludes:
  • The failure is attributable to a specific earlier stage, which takes precedence

D. Severity

How bad the consequence was — 4 categories

D1_blocking — Execution cannot continue; crash, exception, or hard stop
Execution cannot continue: an unhandled exception, crash or hard stop, with no usable deliverable.
Includes:
  • The run aborts with an exception
  • The process exits or hangs until killed
  • No output is produced at all
Excludes:
  • The run completes but the deliverable is wrong (D2)
  • The run completes with a workaround or reduced quality (D3)
D2_incorrect_output — Run completes but the deliverable is wrong or silently corrupted
The run completes, but the deliverable is wrong or silently corrupted - the most expensive mode, because nothing signals it.
Includes:
  • A wrong answer, plan or artefact is delivered as if correct
  • Part of the task is silently skipped
  • Output is corrupted but well formed
Excludes:
  • An exception stops the run (D1)
  • Quality is reduced but the output is usable with a workaround (D3)
D3_degraded — Run completes with loss of quality, workaround, or partial output
The run completes with a loss of quality, a workaround, or partial output that remains usable.
Includes:
  • A fallback path or manual workaround is required
  • Output covers only part of the requested task
  • The result is slower or noisier but correct
Excludes:
  • Nothing usable is produced (D1)
  • The delivered result is wrong rather than merely reduced (D2)
D4_minor — Cosmetic, noisy logging, or non-blocking annoyance
Cosmetic or non-blocking: noisy logging, warnings, or formatting issues that do not change the result.
Includes:
  • Warnings or deprecation notices with no functional effect
  • Log noise or duplicated messages
  • Formatting or typography defects in output
Excludes:
  • The result or the availability of the run changes (D1, D2 or D3)

E. Detection point

Who noticed, and when — 5 categories

E1_framework_runtime — Raised by the framework or runtime as an exception
The framework or runtime raised the failure itself, as an exception or a stop.
Includes:
  • An exception is surfaced to the caller
  • The framework logs an error and halts
  • A guard in the runtime rejects the call
Excludes:
  • The run finishes and a human notices the output is wrong (E3)
E2_external_test — Caught by a test, evaluation harness, or assertion
A test, evaluation harness or assertion caught it, including CI.
Includes:
  • A unit or integration test fails
  • An evaluation harness score drops below its threshold
  • A CI assertion rejects the build
Excludes:
  • The product runtime raised it while running for a user (E1)
E3_human_observation — Noticed by a human inspecting output or behaviour
A person noticed it by inspecting output or behaviour, with no automated signal.
Includes:
  • A user reports a wrong answer or a bad plan
  • A reviewer spots the defect in the output
  • The reporter found it while using the application
Excludes:
  • An automated monitor or alert found it (E4)
  • A test found it before release (E2)
E4_production_monitoring — Detected by logging, metrics, or alerting in operation
Logging, metrics or alerting detected it in operation.
Includes:
  • An alert fired on an error rate or latency metric
  • A dashboard or log review exposed the failure
  • Tracing identified the failing step in production
Excludes:
  • It was caught in a test rather than in operation (E2)
E5_configuration_validation — Caught during setup or configuration validation
A preflight or configuration check caught it during setup.
Includes:
  • A start-up validation rejects the configuration
  • A credential or connectivity check fails before any call
  • A schema check on configuration refuses to start
Excludes:
  • The error is raised later during a call (E1)

Coding rules

The precedence order applied when more than one category appears to fit.

R1 - Exception decides
If the report contains a Python exception, the component that raised it decides dimension A. TypeError on a call signature is A3; ValidationError is A6; a tool-registry error is A2.
R2 - Tool beats compatibility
When a failure concerns a tool call whose arguments fail validation, code A2, not A6, because the agent-tool interface is the failing mechanism.
R3 - Communication requires two agents
A4 applies only when the report describes an exchange between agents. A single agent looping internally is A1.
R4 - Never force a label
If the evidence supports no category with at least moderate confidence, code A10/B10 and record the reason. Unknown records stay in every denominator unless explicitly excluded.
R5 - Cause separate from type
Dimension B must not restate dimension A. A3 (type) can be caused by B2 (version drift) or B1 (framework defect); record which.

Research questions and agent assignment

A question is assigned to a single agent only when one pass over one table answers it. Questions that require deriving a variable, testing an association and then checking the claim against the source records are assigned to a chain, because the verification step is what prevents unsupported numbers from reaching a report.

RQ1. What is the distribution of failure types across agentic applications?agent chain
Frequency table with Wilson 95% CIs; denominator = retained failure records. · TaggerAgent, StatisticianAgent
24.2% of records are functionality / reasoning defect.
RQ2. Which failure types dominate, and how precisely is dominance estimated?agent chain
Ranking with CIs, plus a sensitivity analysis restricted to high-confidence labels. · TaggerAgent, StatisticianAgent, CriticAgent
Restricting to confident labels leaves the ranking unchanged.
RQ3. Which causes are associated with which failure types?agent chain
Contingency analysis, chi-square with Cramer's V, BH-corrected p-values, and lift per cell. · TaggerAgent, CausalAgent, CriticAgent
V = 0.373; 374 causes are demonstrated.
RQ4. Do frameworks differ in their mix of failure types?agent chain
Chi-square across frameworks; per-framework composition reported descriptively. · TaggerAgent, ComparatorAgent, StatisticianAgent
No two frameworks share a dominant category (V = 0.261).
RQ5. Does framework choice affect the rate of blocking-severity failures?agent chain
Blocking-rate per framework with Wilson CIs; pairwise Fisher tests; BH correction. · TaggerAgent, ComparatorAgent, StatisticianAgent, CriticAgent
Blocking rate spans 36.5% to 96.0%.
RQ6. Does declared agent complexity increase the likelihood of orchestration or context failures?agent chain
Complexity index (0-3) derived from reported architecture; trend test across tiers. · ComplexityAgent, StatisticianAgent, CriticAgent
Orchestration/context share rises from 2.6% to 32.7% across tiers.
RQ7. Are some failure types more likely to escape to users rather than be caught at runtime?agent chain
Escape rate = share not detected by framework runtime, tested across types. · TaggerAgent, StatisticianAgent
31.9% of failures escape runtime detection.
RQ8. How much of the corpus cannot be classified, and does that vary by framework?single agent
Unknown share with CIs per framework; lexical-coverage discussion. · StatisticianAgent
Coverage is 97.0%; unknowns stay in every denominator.
RQ9. Has the failure mix changed as the frameworks matured?agent chain
Failure composition by year with a chi-square trend; requires adequate per-year n. · TaggerAgent, ComparatorAgent, StatisticianAgent
Composition changed over time (V = 0.113), confounded by collection.
RQ10. Which failure types co-occur with tool and orchestration infrastructure?agent chain
Stratified composition: tool-using vs non-tool records; orchestrated vs single-agent records. · ComplexityAgent, CausalAgent, CriticAgent
Tool-heavy stacks move the failure surface to tool contracts (V = 0.338).

How the application is organised

Eight agents on a shared blackboard. Any agent can be re-run in isolation and its contribution inspected.

AgentResponsibility
PlannerMaps each question to the variables, the test and the output shape it requires.
TaggerResolves labels and confidence; exposes the evidence span for each.
StatisticianDistributions, intervals, association tests, corrected p-values.
CausalCause-to-type contingency analysis with lift per cell, graded by evidence.
ComparatorFramework and time contrasts with multiple-testing control.
ComplexityDeclared capability index and trend across tiers.
CriticRecomputes every headline metric on an independent code path; blocks a mismatch.
ReporterAssembles verified results into tables, figures and prose.
In the run shown here, all ten questions passed verification with no rejections.

What the instrument can and cannot support

Five experiments test the labelling instrument rather than the findings. One is still pending, and it is stated as pending rather than approximated.

IDExperimentDesign ResultReading
E1Reference agreementn = 10051.0% exact · macro-F1 0.536 · κ = 0.44Moderate — residual error on two boundaries
E2Perturbation retentionn = 15081.3% (95% CI 74.3–86.8%)Labels survive rewording and anonymisation
E3Exception-rule ablationn = 30892.6% of labels changeNot dependent on pasted tracebacks
E4Confidence calibrationn = 10039% → 60% across binsInformative for triage, not calibrated
E5Blind second coder40 recordspendingRequires a coder independent of the author
Agreement of κ = 0.44 with a first-pass reference annotation is moderate, not high. The residual error concentrates on two codebook boundaries — compatibility versus configuration, and functionality versus output parsing. Those are codebook problems, and they are the agenda for v1.1.

Confusion against reference annotation

Requirement conformance

Every line of the supervisor's checklist, answered with the number that satisfies it. 13 of 16 lines are met and 3 are met with a limit stated in the row. The evidence is read from the same artefacts the report uses, so this page cannot drift from the study.

Supervisor checklist

S1 Show the final failure taxonomy, the definitions of each category, and how the categories were derived or manually classified. Met
37 codes across 5 dimensions (A=10, B=10, C=8, D=4, E=5); every code has a definition, an inclusion rule and an explicit exclusion clause, and the loader refuses to start if any is missing.
Answered in: taxonomy.v1.yaml (frozen v1.0, all 37 boundaries documented); report section 4 and 4.1-4.4 (tables 4.1-4.5); derivation narrative in section 4.5; application tab 'Taxonomy'.
S2 Traceable examples from real datasets or logs for each taxonomy category. Met
49 exemplars covering 10 of 10 categories; each row carries record id, repository, issue number, URL and the evidence span that produced the label.
Answered in: taxonomy_exemplars.csv; report section 4.6 with the per-category table; application tab 'Taxonomy'.
S3 Explicit research questions RQ1..RQn (2-10), not only dashboard questions. Met
10 numbered research questions, each with a rationale, required variables, method, and named output artefact. 9 use a chain of agents, 1 a single agent.
Answered in: research_questions.yaml; report section 6; paper section 3; application tab 'Research questions'.
S4 State which research question uses a single agent, which uses multiple agents, and why. Met
Every one of the 10 questions declares agent_mode (single|chain) and the ordered list of agents that answer it; the assignment rule is stated in the config header and justified per question.
Answered in: research_questions.yaml; report section 6.1 (assignment rule) and the per-question table; application tab 'Research questions' shows the same pairing at runtime.
S5 Prove the dataset size (hundreds of failure records). Met
N = 3,089 retained failure records after exclusion; 8 public repositories; 8 frameworks; 2023-2026. Exclusions are counted and stored with a reason per record.
Answered in: failures.jsonl (27 fields); dataset_sources.csv; report section 5; paper Table 1.
S6 Document public dataset sources (Hugging Face, AI-dev datasets, CrewAI/AutoGen/LangGraph, GitHub issues and logs). Met
8 public GitHub repositories across 8 frameworks, with per-source counts, date ranges and traceback coverage. The source-selection rationale is stated, and the corpus is now published as a Hugging Face dataset with a schema, a codebook, a licence and a card that states its limits. AIDev (hao-li/AIDev) is used as a second, independent corpus: 361,296 agent-authored pull requests across 25,403 repositories, analysed at the outcome level in report section 9.8.
Answered in: dataset_sources.csv; report sections 5.1 and 9.8; aidev_agent_outcomes.csv; aidev_validation.json; outputs/hf_dataset/ (dataset card, parquet, codebook); deploy/push_hf.py (publish path); data/raw/ retains the collected payload.
S7 Document how the taxonomy and the dataset actually enter the application. Met
The taxonomy is loaded from taxonomy.v1.yaml at process start; the dataset is loaded from failures.jsonl (3,089 rows). Both are required arguments to the orchestrator, not hard-coded.
Answered in: taxonomy.py, analysis.py, agents.py; report section 7.1; outputs/app/service/ for the deployed instance.
S8 Architecture showing what every agent does. Met
8 agents on a shared blackboard: Planner, Tagger, Statistician, Causal, Comparator, Complexity, Critic, Exporter. Each declares its goal, its inputs and the functions it may call; the critic can reject a table.
Answered in: agents.py; report section 7.2 with the agent table; application tab 'How it works' streams the same trace live.
S9 Statistical results, tables, percentages and visual reports. Met
Every question has a table with denominators, Wilson 95% CIs, effect size and corrected p-values; figures are generated from the same verified results object.
Answered in: tables/, figures/, analysis_results.json; report section 8; paper section 4.
S10 Tables, percentages and visual reports tied to a research question. Met
All 10 questions produce a named primary output; each report subsection states the question it answers in its heading (e.g. '8.5 Framework differences (RQ4)').
Answered in: Report section 8.1-8.11; analysis_report.md.
S11 Report the most common failures as a result tied to a research question. Met
RQ1: Functionality / reasoning defect is the largest category at 748 of 3,089 records (24.2%) with a Wilson 95% CI; the full ranking with CIs is reported alongside.
Answered in: Report section 8.1 (RQ1) and 8.2 (RQ2 sensitivity); figure 1.
S12 Main causes of failures, as an explicit root-cause classification rather than only failure categories. Met with stated limit
A second, separate dimension (B) codes cause class with 10 codes; its association with failure type is tested with Cramer's V and BH-corrected p-values. Evidence is graded demonstrated / supported / hypothesised.
Answered in: taxonomy.v1.yaml dimension B; report section 8.4 (RQ3); paper section 4.4.
S13 Quantitative comparison of frameworks based on the dataset. Met
RQ4 tests the framework x failure-type table (chi-square, Cramer's V); RQ5 compares blocking-severity rates with Wilson CIs and pairwise Fisher tests. Leave-one-framework-out confirms the association is not produced by one repository.
Answered in: Report sections 8.5 and 8.6; leave_one_framework_out.csv.
S14 A measurable definition of agent complexity and an analysis if the complexity RQ is retained. Met with stated limit
Index 0-3 = sum of three binary declared capabilities (multi_agent, uses_tools, uses_memory) with fixed lexicons. Tier counts: 0=699, 1=1258, 2=921, 3=211. Each component separately tracks orchestration/context failure (differences multi_agent +16.6pp, uses_tools +3.9pp, uses_memory +20.0pp).
Answered in: complexity.py; complexity_definition.json; report section 8.8; paper section 4.6.
S15 Simple experiments for validation. Met
Two experiment suites are reported. Instrument suite E1-E5: reference agreement, perturbation robustness, structural-cue ablation, confidence calibration, second-coder protocol. Finding suite F1-F4: resampling, temporal holdout, leave-one-framework-out, label-noise sensitivity.
Answered in: validation.py, findings_validation.py; report sections 9 and 10; findings_validation.json.
S16 Demonstrate how the classification and the results were checked. Met with stated limit
Instrument: exact agreement 51.0% (macro-F1 0.536, kappa 0.44) on n=100; perturbation retention 81.3%. Findings: 5 claims tested - 2 stable, 2 direction-stable, 1 not stable.
Answered in: Report section 9 (instrument) and section 10 (findings); validation_summary.json, findings_validation.json.

Response to the requirements document

#ObjectiveStatusEvidence
O1Conduct an empirical study establishing a taxonomy of failures in agentic applications and identify their causes.MetN = 3,089 records; 5 dimensions; cause class coded separately and graded.
O2The taxonomy classifies different types of failure, e.g. functionality, data structure, tool-related; the first step is to identify all classes.Met10 failure-type codes including functionality (A1), data structure (A6) and tool-related (A2); classes were identified before being counted, and the identification step is documented.
O3After the taxonomy, analyse the causes of each type of failure by exploring the datasets.Met with stated limitCause-by-type contingency analysis with Cramer's V, lift per cell and BH correction; evidence grading separates demonstrated mechanisms from hypotheses.
O4Use existing public datasets from AI development to analyse and draw statistics on failures.Met8 public repositories, 8 frameworks, 2023-2026, with per-source provenance and a permalink per record. The corpus is released as a Hugging Face dataset (parquet, 32 columns, codebook and card) so it can be loaded with load_dataset alongside the datasets it is compared with.
O5Build an application or agents that facilitate the empirical study and answer specific research questions.Met8-agent orchestrator answering 10 questions; deployed web application with live execution trace, corpus search and export.
O6Formulate specific research questions: most common failures, framework relationship, causes related to functionality and complexity.Met10 questions covering frequency (RQ1-2), cause (RQ3), framework (RQ4-5), complexity (RQ6), detection (RQ7), coverage (RQ8), time (RQ9) and tool/orchestration strata (RQ10).
O7Methodology clarification: the taxonomy may be established manually, with agents used to extract data and answers.MetThe codebook is human-authored and frozen before labelling; agents do the extraction, tabulation and verification. The division of labour is stated explicitly.
O8Support each category with real examples from datasets and logs.Met49 cited exemplars across 10 categories, each with a URL.
O9Generate statistical results, tables, percentages and visual reports.MetTables with denominators and Wilson CIs; figures regenerated from verified results.
O10Validate findings through simple experiments where possible.Met with stated limitTwo suites (E1-E5 instrument, F1-F4 findings). One claim is reported as not stable; that outcome is used, not suppressed.

Validation of the findings

The instrument is validated above. These four tests check whether a conclusion survives a different draw, a later corpus, the removal of any single repository, and the measured label error rate. 2 of 5 claims are stable; 1 is not, and is reported as such.

IDTestResultVerdict
F1Resampling stabilitytop category retained in 100.0% of 1,000 replicatesstable
F2Temporal holdoutbefore/after 2025: V = 0.30, top-three overlap 0.20not stable
F3Leave one framework outtop category unchanged in 8 of 8 exclusionsstable
F4Label-noise sensitivityerror rate 49%; top category retained in 100.0%direction stable, magnitude uncertain

Where the data comes from

The brief names candidate sources rather than mandating one. Each is accounted for below: whether it was used, and if not, why not. A source that is silently omitted is the thing this table exists to prevent.

Candidate sourceUsed?Reason
GitHub issue trackers of LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, AutoGPT, LlamaIndex, OpenAI-Agents, MetaGPT, SWE-agentYesGives a permalink per failure, which is what traceability requires, and covers all four failure classes the brief names.
AIDev (hao-li/AIDev) — pull requests authored by coding agentsYesThe second corpus. AIDev is a census of pull requests written by OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Devin and Google Jules in real repositories, so its rows were not selected for being failures. Used for an outcome-level check that does not depend on the labeller: 361,296 agent-authored pull requests across 25,403 repositories, whether each merged, was closed unmerged, or was rejected by a human reviewer. Not used to label dimension A, because a review comment is not a failure report.
Hugging Face Hub — aggregated failure datasetsAs outputThe publication target for this study's own corpus, and the host of the AIDev tables above. No aggregated set of agentic-application failure reports was found whose rows resolve to a citable source, so one could not be used as input: a label would have had no report to be checked against.
AI-development datasets generally (beyond AIDev)NoCurated for repository and commit metadata of human activity, or for task completion rather than failure; only AIDev records what agents actually produced in public repositories.
LangGraph and CrewAI logs (private)NoNot public: projects do not release logs of real runs, and inventing them would break the traceability rule.
Discord / Slack community logsNoNot public, not citable, and not redistributable.

An independent corpus: agent-authored pull requests

361,296 pull requests written by coding agents in 25,403 real repositories (AIDev), none of them selected for being failures. Used as an outcome-level check that does not touch the labeller or the codebook.

AgentPRsMerged Closed unmergedChanges requested
Claude Code172,59771.8%21.2%2.3%
Copilot98,38460.6%34.3%6.5%
OpenAI Codex62,73175.2%20.1%0.8%
Cursor12,90857.9%36.0%0.9%
Devin11,21958.8%38.1%4.8%
Google Jules3,45760.0%35.9%2.5%

Outcome-level only. AIDev records pull requests authored by coding agents in real repositories, so the rows were not selected for being failures. Closed-unmerged is an upper bound on failure, not an estimate: a pull request can be closed because it was superseded. Changes-requested counts style and scope disagreements with real defects. The taxonomy is not applied to these rows, because a review comment is not a failure report.

Every record shown here is traceable to a public bug report, and the original report is linked from it. Users sometimes paste their own API keys into those reports; any credential-shaped string is therefore masked as [redacted: credential] on this page. The stored corpus is left unmodified so the text still matches the source it cites, and it is not published.

Record schema

One JSON object per line in the corpus file; the CSV carries the same fields.

FieldMeaning
record_idStable hash; the join key across all artefacts.
repo, issue_number, urlProvenance — the original report.
created_at, year, state, labelsTracker context.
A_failure_type, A_confidence, A_evidencePrimary dimension, confidence, and the text span that produced the label.
B_cause_class, B_evidence_gradeStated cause, graded demonstrated / supported / hypothesised.
C_lifecycle_stage, D_severity, E_detection_pointRemaining three dimensions.
matched_rules, taxonomy_versionAudit trail: which rules fired, against which codebook.

Reproducing the analysis

From the project root, with PYTHONPATH=src set:

python -m afs.cli build      # normalise + label
python -m afs.cli analyze    # multi-agent pipeline with critic verification
python -m afs.cli validate   # validation experiments
python -m afs.cli export     # Word report
python -m afs.cli paper      # journal-style manuscript
python -m afs.cli app        # this page
Regenerating the corpus is deterministic: the labeller is rule-based, so the same text yields the same label and the same evidence span. Collection is rate-limited by the public API and takes about six minutes; every later stage is offline.
